# Unit 1: Fluids

## Overview
This unit introduces how **fluids** behave at rest and in motion, focusing on **pressure**, **buoyant force**, the **continuity equation**, and **Bernoulli’s principle**. These ideas are heavily tested on the AP Physics 2 exam because they connect conceptual reasoning, algebraic modeling, and real-world situations such as floating objects, fluid flow in pipes, and pressure differences in liquids and gases.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Density** | Mass per unit volume of a substance. | Used to compare substances, determine whether objects float or sink, and calculate buoyant force and pressure effects. |
| **Pressure** | Force distributed over an area. | Central to explaining fluid statics, hydraulics, and why pressure changes with depth. |
| **Hydrostatic Pressure** | Pressure in a fluid due to the weight of the fluid above it. | Frequently appears in problems involving depth, open containers, and manometers. |
| **Pascal’s Principle** | A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid. | Explains hydraulic lifts and force multiplication; AP questions often test area-force relationships. |
| **Buoyancy** | Upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object. | Essential for floating, sinking, and submerged-object problems; tied directly to **Archimedes’ principle**. |
| **Continuity Equation** | Relationship showing conservation of mass in flowing fluids. | Used to compare speed and cross-sectional area in pipes; often paired with Bernoulli reasoning. |
| **Bernoulli’s Principle** | Relates pressure, speed, and height in streamline fluid flow. | A major AP concept for understanding why faster-moving fluid can correspond to lower pressure. |
| **Ideal vs. Real Fluids** | Ideal fluids are incompressible and nonviscous; real fluids may have viscosity and turbulence. | AP questions often assume ideal fluid conditions, so students must recognize model assumptions. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Fluid at rest or in motion"] --> B["Determine situation type"]
    B --> C["Static fluid"]
    B --> D["Moving fluid"]

    C --> E["Use pressure ideas"]
    E --> F["$$P = \\frac{F}{A}$$"]
    E --> G["$$P = P_0 + \\rho g h$$"]
    E --> H["Compare depths and surfaces"]

    C --> I["Check for buoyancy"]
    I --> J["Displaced fluid creates upward force"]
    J --> K["$$F_B = \\rho_{fluid} g V_{disp}$$"]
    K --> L["Float, sink, or remain suspended?"]

    D --> M["Use conservation of mass"]
    M --> N["$$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$"]

    D --> O["Use energy per unit volume"]
    O --> P["$$P + \\frac{1}{2}\\rho v^2 + \\rho g y = \\text{constant}$$"]
    P --> Q["Relate pressure, speed, and height"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Quantity** | **Expression** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Density** | $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$ | Relates mass and volume; useful for fluid identification and buoyancy. |
| **Pressure** | $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$ | Pressure increases when force increases or area decreases. |
| **Hydrostatic Pressure** | $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$ | Pressure at depth $$h$$ in a fluid open to the atmosphere. |
| **Pressure Difference** | $$\Delta P = \rho g \Delta h$$ | Useful when comparing two points in the same fluid. |
| **Pascal’s Principle** | $$P_1 = P_2 \Rightarrow \frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$ | Basis for hydraulic systems. |
| **Buoyant Force** | $$F_B = \rho_{fluid} g V_{disp}$$ | Weight of the displaced fluid. |
| **Floating Condition** | $$F_B = mg$$ | For an object floating in equilibrium. |
| **Continuity Equation** | $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$ | For steady flow of an incompressible fluid. |
| **Bernoulli’s Equation** | $$P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g y = \text{constant}$$ | Connects pressure, speed, and height along a streamline. |
| **Special Bernoulli Comparison** | $$P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g y_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g y_2$$ | Compare two locations in the same moving fluid. |

**Must-know rules and assumptions:**
- **Pressure in a static fluid** depends on **depth**, not container shape.
- In the same connected static fluid, points at the same depth have the same pressure.
- **Buoyant force** depends on the **fluid displaced**, not directly on the object’s total mass.
- **Continuity** and **Bernoulli** usually assume an **ideal fluid**: incompressible, nonviscous, and steady flow.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **How They Are Connected** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Pressure vs. Force** | Pressure is created by force acting over an area. | **Force** is measured in newtons; **pressure** is force per area. |
| **Hydrostatic Pressure vs. Bernoulli Pressure Effects** | Both involve pressure in fluids. | Hydrostatic pressure comes from fluid weight at depth; Bernoulli describes pressure changes due to speed and height in moving fluids. |
| **Buoyancy vs. Weight** | Both are forces acting on an object in a fluid. | **Weight** acts downward due to gravity; **buoyant force** acts upward due to displaced fluid. |
| **Continuity vs. Bernoulli** | Both describe moving fluids and are often used together. | Continuity comes from **mass conservation**; Bernoulli comes from **energy conservation**. |

### Useful conceptual comparison
- In a **narrower pipe**, fluid speed is typically **greater** because of $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$.
- If height is unchanged, greater speed usually means **lower pressure** by Bernoulli’s principle.
- This does **not** mean “moving fluids always have low pressure”; pressure depends on the full balance of speed, height, and surrounding conditions.

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **pressure** with **force**. A larger pressure does not necessarily mean a larger total force unless the area is also considered.
- Assuming pressure depends on the **shape** or total volume of the container. In hydrostatics, pressure at a point depends on $$\rho$$, $$g$$, and $$h$$.
- Forgetting that **buoyant force** is based on the **displaced fluid volume**, not always the object’s full volume. For floating objects, only part of the object may be submerged.
- Reversing the continuity relationship: when area decreases, **speed increases**, not decreases.
- Using **Bernoulli’s equation** between points that are not on the same streamline or in situations where viscosity, turbulence, or pumps make the ideal model invalid.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can define **density** and use $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$ in fluid problems.
- [ ] I can calculate **pressure** from force and area using $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$.
- [ ] I can explain why pressure in a fluid increases with depth using $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$.
- [ ] I can apply **Pascal’s principle** to hydraulic systems and relate forces to areas.
- [ ] I can calculate **buoyant force** and determine whether an object floats, sinks, or is neutrally buoyant.
- [ ] I can use $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$ to compare fluid speeds in different parts of a pipe.
- [ ] I can apply **Bernoulli’s equation** to relate pressure, speed, and height in moving fluids.
- [ ] I can distinguish when to use **fluid statics** ideas versus **fluid dynamics** ideas on an AP-style problem.

# Unit 2: Thermodynamics

## Overview
This unit studies how **energy** moves and changes form through **heat**, **work**, and the behavior of **gases**. For the AP Physics 2 exam, you must connect particle-level ideas from **kinetic theory** to macroscopic laws like the **ideal gas law**, the **first law of thermodynamics**, and the **second law of thermodynamics**, especially in reasoning about **engines**, **efficiency**, and **entropy**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Ideal Gas Law** | Relationship among **pressure**, **volume**, **temperature**, and amount of gas: $$PV=nRT$$ | Frequently used to predict how a gas changes during heating, cooling, compression, or expansion |
| **Kinetic Theory** | Model that explains gas behavior by the motion of many tiny particles | Lets you justify why temperature relates to average molecular kinetic energy |
| **Internal Energy** | Total microscopic energy of a system; for an ideal gas, it depends only on temperature | Essential for applying the **first law** and comparing thermodynamic states |
| **First Law of Thermodynamics** | Energy conservation for thermal systems: heat added can change internal energy and/or do work | One of the most common free-response and multiple-choice tools in this unit |
| **PV Diagrams and Work** | Graphical representation of thermodynamic processes; area under a curve gives work done by the gas | AP questions often ask students to interpret processes visually and compare work values |
| **Second Law of Thermodynamics** | Natural processes increase overall entropy; heat does not spontaneously flow from cold to hot | Explains why no engine can be $$100\%$$ efficient and why some processes are irreversible |
| **Heat Engines** | Devices that convert thermal energy into useful work by operating between hot and cold reservoirs | You must calculate efficiency and reason about energy flow in cyclic processes |
| **Entropy** | Measure of energy dispersal or number of possible microscopic arrangements | Used conceptually to determine whether a process is spontaneous or reversible |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Gas system in an initial state"] --> B["Energy transfer occurs as heat: $$Q$$"]
    A --> C["Energy transfer occurs as work: $$W$$"]
    B --> D["Internal energy changes: $$\Delta U$$"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["State variables may change: $$P$$, $$V$$, $$T$$"]
    E --> F["Process shown on a $$PV$$ diagram"]
    F --> G["For a cycle, system may return to initial state"]
    G --> H["Over a full cycle: $$\Delta U = 0$$"]
    H --> I["Net heat input becomes net work output"]
    I --> J["Heat engine efficiency limited by second law and entropy increase"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Quantity** | **Expression / Definition** | **What to Remember** |
|---|---|---|
| **Ideal Gas Law** | $$PV=nRT$$ | Connects the macroscopic state variables of an ideal gas |
| **Pressure from force** | $$P=\frac{F}{A}$$ | Useful foundation for understanding gas pressure |
| **Average translational kinetic energy** | $$K_{\text{avg}}=\frac{3}{2}k_B T$$ | Temperature measures average kinetic energy per molecule |
| **Internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas** | $$U=\frac{3}{2}nRT$$ | For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature |
| **First law of thermodynamics** | $$\Delta U = Q - W$$ | Here, $$W$$ is work done **by the system** |
| **Work done by a gas** | $$W=\int P\,dV$$ | On a $$PV$$ diagram, this is the area under the curve |
| **Constant-pressure work** | $$W=P\Delta V$$ | Valid only if pressure remains constant |
| **Efficiency of a heat engine** | $$e=\frac{W}{Q_H}=1-\frac{Q_C}{Q_H}$$ | Always less than $$1$$ |
| **Second law of thermodynamics** | No cyclic engine can convert all absorbed heat into work | Some energy must be rejected to a colder reservoir |
| **Entropy change for a reversible process** | $$\Delta S=\frac{Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$$ | Entropy helps determine reversibility and spontaneity |
| **Thermal efficiency limit for an ideal reversible engine** | $$e_{\text{max}}=1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}$$ | Temperatures must be in **kelvins** |

### Important process types
- **Isothermal process**: temperature constant, so for an ideal gas $$\Delta U=0$$.
- **Isochoric process**: volume constant, so $$W=0$$.
- **Isobaric process**: pressure constant, so $$W=P\Delta V$$.
- **Adiabatic process**: no heat transfer, so $$Q=0$$.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **How They’re Connected** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Heat** vs. **Temperature** | Both relate to thermal behavior | **Temperature** measures average kinetic energy; **heat** is energy transferred due to temperature difference |
| **Internal Energy** vs. **Heat** | Heat transfer can change internal energy | **Internal energy** is stored in the system; **heat** is energy in transit |
| **Work** vs. **Heat** | Both are methods of energy transfer | **Work** transfers energy by macroscopic force through distance; **heat** transfers energy because of temperature difference |
| **First Law** vs. **Second Law** | Both govern thermodynamic systems | **First law** says energy is conserved; **second law** limits direction of processes and efficiency |
| **Reversible** vs. **Irreversible** processes | Both describe thermodynamic changes | **Reversible** processes are idealized and entropy-neutral for the universe; **irreversible** ones increase total entropy |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Hot reservoir at $$T_H$$"] --> B["Heat input $$Q_H$$"]
    B --> C["Engine"]
    C --> D["Work output $$W$$"]
    C --> E["Heat expelled $$Q_C$$"]
    E --> F["Cold reservoir at $$T_C$$"]
    D --> G["Useful mechanical output"]
    F --> H["Second law requires $$Q_C > 0$$ for any real engine"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **heat** with **temperature**. A system can have a high temperature without transferring heat unless there is a temperature difference.
- Forgetting the sign convention in $$\Delta U = Q - W$$. If the gas does work on the surroundings, then $$W>0$$ and the system loses internal energy unless heat is added.
- Using Celsius instead of **kelvins** in gas law or efficiency calculations. Absolute temperature must be used in equations such as $$PV=nRT$$ and $$e_{\text{max}}=1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}$$.
- Assuming internal energy always changes when pressure or volume changes. For an **ideal gas**, internal energy depends only on temperature.
- Thinking a larger area on a $$PV$$ diagram always means more heat transferred. The area under the curve corresponds to **work**, not necessarily heat.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can apply the **ideal gas law** $$PV=nRT$$ to solve for a missing variable.
- [ ] I can explain how **kinetic theory** connects temperature to particle motion and average kinetic energy.
- [ ] I can use the **first law of thermodynamics** $$\Delta U = Q - W$$ with correct signs.
- [ ] I can determine the **work done by a gas** from a process description or a $$PV$$ diagram.
- [ ] I can identify **isothermal**, **isochoric**, **isobaric**, and **adiabatic** processes and state what remains constant in each.
- [ ] I can calculate or compare **heat engine efficiency** using $$e=\frac{W}{Q_H}=1-\frac{Q_C}{Q_H}$$.
- [ ] I can explain why the **second law of thermodynamics** prevents a perfectly efficient engine.
- [ ] I can reason qualitatively about **entropy** and decide whether a process is more reversible or more spontaneous.

multipleChoice.questionText: A rigid container holds an ideal gas. The absolute temperature of the gas is doubled while the amount of gas remains constant. Which statement correctly describes the gas?
options: The pressure doubles because $$P\propto T$$ when $$V$$ and $$n$$ are constant.
The pressure remains constant because the volume does not change.
The average kinetic energy of the molecules remains constant because the container is rigid.
The pressure is cut in half because collisions become less frequent at higher temperature.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The pressure doubles because $$P\propto T$$ when $$V$$ and $$n$$ are constant.

multipleChoice.questionText: Two sealed containers hold different ideal gases at the same absolute temperature. Container A has particles of mass $$m$$, and container B has particles of mass $$4m$$. Which comparison is correct?
options: The particles in A have twice the root-mean-square speed of the particles in B.
The particles in B have twice the average translational kinetic energy of the particles in A.
The particles in A have four times the average translational kinetic energy of the particles in B.
The particles in both containers have the same root-mean-square speed because the temperatures are equal.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The particles in A have twice the root-mean-square speed of the particles in B.

# Unit 3: Electric Force, Field, and Potential

## Overview
This unit develops the core ideas of **electrostatics**: how charges interact through **electric force**, how those interactions are described by an **electric field**, and how energy is stored and transferred through **electric potential**. These ideas are heavily tested on the AP Physics 2 exam through conceptual reasoning, multiple representations, and algebraic problem-solving involving **Coulomb’s law**, **Gauss’s law**, and **potential relationships**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Electric charge** | A fundamental property that can be positive or negative; charge is conserved and quantized. | Many AP questions begin with identifying charge interactions and using **conservation of charge** qualitatively. |
| **Coulomb’s law** | The electric force between two point charges depends on the product of the charges and inversely on the square of the distance between them. | Essential for calculating force magnitude/direction and comparing how force changes when distance or charge changes. |
| **Electric field** | A vector field that gives force per unit charge at a point. | AP problems often ask students to distinguish **field** from **force** and determine field direction due to charge arrangements. |
| **Electric field lines** | A visual model showing field direction and relative strength. | Frequently used in conceptual questions about symmetry, relative magnitude, and motion of test charges. |
| **Gauss’s law** | The net electric flux through a closed surface depends on enclosed charge. | On the AP exam, this is mainly used conceptually and with high-symmetry situations to connect **flux** and **charge enclosed**. |
| **Electric potential energy** | Energy associated with the configuration of charges in an electric system. | Important for analyzing work, energy changes, and motion in electric fields. |
| **Electric potential** | Potential energy per unit charge; a scalar quantity. | Students must connect **potential**, **work**, and **field**, especially when comparing points in space. |
| **Equipotential surfaces** | Surfaces where electric potential is constant. | AP questions often test the relationship between **equipotentials** and **electric field direction**. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Charges create electric interactions] --> B[Use Coulomb's law for force between point charges]
    A --> C[Define electric field as force per unit charge]
    C --> D[Represent field with vectors or field lines]
    D --> E[Use symmetry and flux ideas with Gauss's law]
    C --> F[Connect field to changes in electric potential]
    F --> G[Relate potential to potential energy]
    G --> H[Use energy ideas to predict motion, work, and system changes]
```

A useful problem-solving progression for this unit is:

1. **Identify the source charges** and whether the question asks about **force**, **field**, **potential**, or **energy**.
2. Decide whether the quantity is **vector** or **scalar**.
   - **Force** and **electric field** are vectors.
   - **Potential** and **potential energy** are scalars.
3. Choose the right model:
   - **Coulomb’s law** for force between point charges
   - **Superposition** for multiple charges
   - **Gauss’s law** for symmetric charge distributions
   - **Energy/potential equations** for work and motion
4. Check direction, sign, and units.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Relationship** | **Formula / Rule** | **What to Remember** |
|---|---|---|
| **Coulomb’s law** | $$F = k\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$$ | Force is attractive for opposite charges and repulsive for like charges. |
| **Electric field definition** | $$\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q}$$ | Field direction is the direction of force on a **positive** test charge. |
| **Field from a point charge** | $$E = k\frac{|q|}{r^2}$$ | For a positive source charge, field points outward; for a negative source charge, inward. |
| **Superposition** | $$\vec{E}_{\text{net}} = \sum \vec{E}_i$$ | Add electric fields as vectors. |
| **Electric flux** | $$\Phi_E = \vec{E}\cdot \vec{A} = EA\cos\theta$$ | Flux depends on field strength, area, and orientation. |
| **Gauss’s law** | $$\Phi_E = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}$$ | Only **enclosed charge** affects net flux through a closed surface. |
| **Electric potential energy of two point charges** | $$U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}$$ | Sign matters: opposite charges give negative potential energy. |
| **Electric potential** | $$V = \frac{U}{q}$$ | Potential is energy per unit charge. |
| **Potential from a point charge** | $$V = k\frac{q}{r}$$ | Potential is scalar, so contributions add algebraically. |
| **Potential difference and work** | $$\Delta V = \frac{\Delta U}{q}$$ and $$W = -\Delta U$$ | Electric forces do positive work when potential energy decreases. |
| **Uniform field and potential difference** | $$\Delta V = -Ed$$ | Valid when displacement is parallel to a uniform field. |
| **Field and equipotentials** | The electric field is perpendicular to equipotential surfaces. | No work is done moving along an equipotential. |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Pair** | **Similarities** | **Key Difference** | **AP Reminder** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Electric force** vs. **electric field** | Both describe electric interactions and have direction. | **Force** depends on the test charge: $$\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$$. **Field** exists whether or not a test charge is present. | Do not confuse the source-created field with the force experienced by a specific charge. |
| **Electric potential energy** vs. **electric potential** | Both relate to energy in electric systems. | **Potential energy** depends on the actual charge placed in the field; **potential** does not. | A point can have a high or low **potential** independent of the test charge chosen. |
| **Field lines** vs. **equipotential lines/surfaces** | Both represent electric behavior in space. | Field lines show direction of **$$\vec{E}$$**; equipotentials show constant **$$V$$**. | Field lines always cross equipotentials at right angles. |
| **Coulomb’s law** vs. **Gauss’s law** | Both describe effects of electric charge. | Coulomb’s law is often used for point charges; Gauss’s law is most useful with strong symmetry. | Gauss’s law is always true, but not always the easiest way to calculate **$$E$$**. |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- **Mixing up scalar and vector quantities**: **electric field** and **force** require direction and vector addition, while **electric potential** adds algebraically.
- **Assuming zero net enclosed charge means zero field everywhere**: A Gaussian surface with $$q_{\text{enc}} = 0$$ has zero **net flux**, but the field at points on the surface may still be nonzero.
- **Using the sign incorrectly in energy and potential**: For opposite charges, $$U$$ is negative; for a negative source charge, $$V$$ is negative.
- **Believing field lines can cross**: If they crossed, the field would have two directions at one point, which is impossible.
- **Forgetting that moving along an equipotential requires no work by the electric force**: Since $$\Delta V = 0$$, the electric potential energy does not change.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can apply **Coulomb’s law** to find how electric force changes with charge and distance.
- [ ] I can determine the **direction** of electric force and electric field for positive and negative charges.
- [ ] I can use **superposition** to find the net electric field from multiple charges.
- [ ] I can interpret **electric field line diagrams** and relate line density to field strength.
- [ ] I can explain **electric flux** and use **Gauss’s law** conceptually or with symmetric charge distributions.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **electric potential energy** and **electric potential**.
- [ ] I can calculate or compare **potential** and **potential energy** for point-charge systems.
- [ ] I can explain why **equipotential surfaces** are perpendicular to electric field lines and why no work is done along them.

flashcards.definition: The magnitude of the interaction between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: $$F = k\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$$. The force acts along the line connecting the charges and may be attractive or repulsive depending on the signs.

A vector quantity defined as the force per unit positive test charge at a location: $$\vec{E} = \dfrac{\vec{F}}{q}$$. For a point charge, its magnitude is $$E = k\dfrac{|q|}{r^2}$$ and its direction is away from positive charge and toward negative charge.

The principle stating that the net effect from multiple sources is found by combining the individual contributions. For vectors such as force or field, this requires vector addition of each contribution at the point of interest.

A visual model in which tangent directions show the direction of the field and line density indicates relative magnitude. They begin on positive charge and end on negative charge or at infinity, and they never cross.

# Unit 4: Electric Circuits

## Overview
This unit introduces how **electric current** moves through circuits and how devices like **resistors** and **capacitors** affect that motion. For the AP Physics 2 exam, you must be able to analyze **series and parallel circuits**, apply **Ohm’s law** and **Kirchhoff’s rules**, and explain how energy and charge behave in **steady-state** and **RC circuits**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Current** | The rate of flow of charge through a conductor. | You must connect current to charge flow and use it in circuit calculations. |
| **Resistance** | A measure of how much a material or device opposes current. | Central to predicting how voltage and current relate in circuits. |
| **Ohm’s Law** | The relationship between voltage, current, and resistance for an ohmic resistor. | Frequently tested in both conceptual and quantitative problems. |
| **Series Circuits** | Components arranged in a single path so the same current passes through each. | You must determine equivalent resistance and voltage drops. |
| **Parallel Circuits** | Components connected across the same two points, sharing the same potential difference. | Common AP topic for comparing current distribution and equivalent resistance. |
| **Kirchhoff’s Rules** | Conservation-based rules for current at junctions and voltage around loops. | Essential for analyzing multi-loop or nontrivial circuits. |
| **Capacitance** | The ability of a device to store charge per unit potential difference. | Appears in capacitor networks and energy storage questions. |
| **RC Circuits** | Circuits with resistors and capacitors that show time-dependent charging and discharging. | Important for interpreting transient behavior and exponential change. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Battery provides potential difference"] --> B["Charges move: current forms"]
    B --> C["Resistors oppose current"]
    C --> D["Apply Ohm's law to each element"]
    D --> E["Use series/parallel rules for simplification"]
    E --> F["Use Kirchhoff's rules for complex loops/junctions"]
    F --> G["Find current, voltage, and power in each branch"]
    G --> H["If capacitor is present, charge and current may change with time"]
    H --> I["In RC charging/discharging, use exponential relationships"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Quantity** | **Expression** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Current** | $$I=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$$ | Current is the rate of charge flow. |
| **Ohm’s Law** | $$V=IR$$ | Relates potential difference, current, and resistance for an ohmic resistor. |
| **Resistance from material** | $$R=\rho \frac{L}{A}$$ | Resistance depends on resistivity, length, and cross-sectional area. |
| **Power** | $$P=IV$$ | Rate of energy transfer in a circuit element. |
| **Power forms** | $$P=I^{2}R \qquad P=\frac{V^{2}}{R}$$ | Useful depending on what quantities are known. |
| **Series resistors** | $$R_{\text{eq}}=R_{1}+R_{2}+\cdots$$ | Equivalent resistance increases in series. |
| **Parallel resistors** | $$\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\cdots$$ | Equivalent resistance decreases in parallel. |
| **Junction rule** | $$\sum I_{\text{in}}=\sum I_{\text{out}}$$ | Charge is conserved at a junction. |
| **Loop rule** | $$\sum \Delta V=0$$ | Energy is conserved around any closed loop. |
| **Capacitance** | $$C=\frac{Q}{V}$$ | Defines how much charge is stored per volt. |
| **Capacitors in parallel** | $$C_{\text{eq}}=C_{1}+C_{2}+\cdots$$ | Parallel capacitors add directly. |
| **Capacitors in series** | $$\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}}=\frac{1}{C_{1}}+\frac{1}{C_{2}}+\cdots$$ | Series capacitors reduce equivalent capacitance. |
| **Energy in capacitor** | $$U=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\frac{1}{2}QV=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C}$$ | Energy stored in the electric field of a capacitor. |
| **RC time constant** | $$\tau=RC$$ | Sets the timescale for charging or discharging. |
| **Charging capacitor** | $$Q(t)=CV\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)$$ | Charge grows exponentially toward a maximum. |
| **Charging current** | $$I(t)=\frac{V}{R}e^{-t/RC}$$ | Current decreases as the capacitor charges. |
| **Discharging capacitor** | $$Q(t)=Q_{0}e^{-t/RC}$$ | Stored charge decays exponentially. |

### Must-know qualitative rules
- In a **series circuit**, the **current** is the same through every element.
- In a **parallel circuit**, the **potential difference** across each branch is the same.
- A capacitor in a **steady-state DC circuit** behaves like an **open circuit**.
- At the instant an uncharged capacitor begins charging, it behaves approximately like a **wire** with respect to current path; after a long time, current in that branch goes to zero.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Topic** | **Series** | **Parallel** | **AP Takeaway** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Resistors** | Same **current** through each resistor | Same **voltage** across each branch | Know which quantity stays constant. |
| **Equivalent resistance** | $$R_{\text{eq}}$$ increases as resistors are added | $$R_{\text{eq}}$$ decreases as branches are added | Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest branch resistance. |
| **Capacitors** | Same **charge** on each capacitor | Same **voltage** across each capacitor | Capacitor rules are opposite of resistor rules in many ways. |
| **Equivalent capacitance** | $$C_{\text{eq}}$$ decreases in series | $$C_{\text{eq}}$$ increases in parallel | A very common comparison question. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Resistors in series"] --> B["Same current"]
    A --> C["Voltages add"]
    D["Resistors in parallel"] --> E["Same voltage"]
    D --> F["Currents add"]
    G["Capacitors in series"] --> H["Same charge"]
    G --> I["Voltages add"]
    J["Capacitors in parallel"] --> K["Same voltage"]
    J --> L["Charges add"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing what stays constant in **series** versus **parallel**: for resistors, **current** is the same in series, but **voltage** is the same in parallel.
- Forgetting that **resistor** and **capacitor** combination rules are reversed: resistors add in series, but capacitors add in parallel.
- Assuming a capacitor always allows current in a DC circuit. In **steady state**, a capacitor branch carries **no current**.
- Using **Kirchhoff’s loop rule** with inconsistent sign conventions. Pick a loop direction and treat voltage rises and drops consistently.
- Thinking the battery “supplies current.” More precisely, the battery supplies **potential difference**, and the circuit determines the resulting current.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define **current**, **resistance**, and **capacitance** in words and with equations.
- [ ] Apply **Ohm’s law** $$V=IR$$ to solve for unknown circuit quantities.
- [ ] Find equivalent resistance for **series** and **parallel** resistor networks.
- [ ] Use **Kirchhoff’s junction rule** and **loop rule** to analyze multiloop circuits.
- [ ] Determine how **current** and **voltage** are distributed in series and parallel branches.
- [ ] Calculate **power** and explain where electrical energy is transferred or stored.
- [ ] Find equivalent capacitance for **series** and **parallel** capacitor arrangements.
- [ ] Describe and calculate **charging** and **discharging** behavior in an **RC circuit**, including the meaning of $$\tau=RC$$.

# Unit 5: Magnetism and Electromagnetic Induction

## Overview
This unit develops the ideas of **magnetic fields**, **magnetic forces**, and how changing magnetic conditions produce **induced emf** and **current**. For the AP Physics 2 exam, students must connect field models, force relationships, and induction laws across conceptual reasoning, experimental setups, and algebra-based problem solving.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Magnetic Field** | A vector field that describes the magnetic influence of moving charges, currents, and magnets. | You must interpret field direction, field-line patterns, and how fields affect charges and wires. |
| **Magnetic Force on a Charge** | The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field depends on charge, speed, field strength, and angle. | AP questions often test direction using the **right-hand rule** and whether magnetic force changes speed or only direction. |
| **Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire** | A wire carrying current in a magnetic field experiences a force. | Important for reasoning about motors, wire motion, and force comparisons. |
| **Biot–Savart Law** | A relationship that gives the magnetic field produced by a small current element. | Used conceptually to determine how current geometry affects magnetic field strength and direction. |
| **Magnetic Flux** | A measure of how much magnetic field passes through an area. | Central to **Faraday’s law**; AP problems often ask what changes flux. |
| **Faraday’s Law** | A changing magnetic flux induces an emf in a loop or coil. | One of the most tested ideas in this unit; students must predict when induction occurs and how strong it is. |
| **Lenz’s Law** | The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux that caused it. | Frequently tested as a direction/reasoning question; it explains the negative sign in Faraday’s law. |
| **Inductors / Self-Induction** | A changing current in a circuit can induce an emf in the same circuit or another nearby circuit. | Links magnetism to circuits; AP may ask about energy storage, opposition to changing current, and induced emf. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Current or moving charge produces magnetic field"] --> B["Magnetic field interacts with charge or wire"]
    B --> C["Magnetic force changes motion or pushes wire"]
    A --> D["Magnetic field passes through area of loop"]
    D --> E["Magnetic flux changes"]
    E --> F["Induced emf is produced (Faraday's law)"]
    F --> G["Induced current may flow if circuit is closed"]
    G --> H["Induced magnetic field opposes flux change (Lenz's law)"]
    G --> I["Current change can create self-induced emf in inductor"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Quantity** | **Expression** | **What to Know** |
|---|---|---|
| **Magnetic force on a charge** | $$F_B = qvB\sin\theta$$ | Applies to a charge moving in a magnetic field; maximum at $$\theta = 90^\circ$$ and zero when velocity is parallel to the field. |
| **Magnetic force on a wire** | $$F_B = ILB\sin\theta$$ | For a straight wire segment of length $$L$$ in a uniform field. |
| **Magnetic field from a long straight wire** | $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$ | Field strength decreases with distance $$r$$ from the wire. |
| **Biot–Savart law** | $$dB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\ell \sin\theta}{r^2}$$ | Describes the contribution of a small current element to the magnetic field. |
| **Magnetic flux** | $$\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$$ | Flux depends on field strength, area, and orientation of the area vector. |
| **Faraday’s law** | $$\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$ | A changing magnetic flux induces emf; for $$N$$ turns, $$\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$. |
| **Lenz’s law** | Included by the negative sign in $$\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$ | The induced current opposes the **change** in flux, not necessarily the original field itself. |
| **Inductor emf** | $$\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$$ | An inductor resists changes in current. |
| **Energy stored in an inductor** | $$U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$$ | Magnetic fields can store energy, similar to how capacitors store electric energy. |

### Direction Rules You Must Know
- Use the **right-hand rule** for the direction of **magnetic field** around a current-carrying wire.
- Use the **right-hand rule** for **magnetic force** on a positive charge; reverse the direction for a negative charge.
- For **Lenz’s law**, first identify whether flux is increasing or decreasing, then determine the induced field that opposes that change.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Pair / Relationship** | **Similarities** | **Key Difference** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Electric Field vs. Magnetic Field** | Both are vector fields that exert forces and can store energy. | Electric fields act on charges whether moving or not; magnetic fields act on moving charges or currents. | AP often asks why a stationary charge feels no magnetic force. |
| **Magnetic Force on Charge vs. Electric Force on Charge** | Both can change a particle’s motion. | Electric force can do work and change speed; magnetic force is perpendicular to motion and typically changes direction only. | Critical for reasoning about circular motion and energy changes. |
| **Faraday’s Law vs. Lenz’s Law** | Both describe electromagnetic induction. | Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of induced emf; Lenz’s law gives its direction. | Many free-response and MC questions require both together. |
| **Inductor vs. Resistor** | Both affect current in a circuit. | A resistor opposes current itself; an inductor opposes **changes** in current. | Important in transient circuit reasoning. |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **magnetic field direction** with **magnetic force direction**; they are not generally the same.
- Forgetting that a **stationary charge** experiences no magnetic force because $$v = 0$$ in $$F_B = qvB\sin\theta$$.
- Thinking **Lenz’s law** opposes the existing magnetic field; it actually opposes the **change in magnetic flux**.
- Missing the angle in **flux** calculations: $$\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$$ uses the angle between the field and the **area vector**, not always the plane itself.
- Assuming induction requires a stronger field only; flux can also change because of changing **area**, changing **orientation**, or moving the loop into or out of the field.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can explain what a **magnetic field** is and determine its direction around a straight current-carrying wire.
- [ ] I can calculate or compare **magnetic force** on a moving charge using $$F_B = qvB\sin\theta$$.
- [ ] I can calculate or compare **magnetic force** on a wire using $$F_B = ILB\sin\theta$$.
- [ ] I can use the **right-hand rule** correctly for magnetic field and magnetic force situations.
- [ ] I can explain how **Biot–Savart reasoning** connects current geometry to magnetic field direction and strength.
- [ ] I can calculate **magnetic flux** with $$\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$$ and describe ways flux can change.
- [ ] I can apply **Faraday’s law** and **Lenz’s law** to determine the magnitude and direction of induced emf or current.
- [ ] I can explain what an **inductor** does and use $$\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$$ and $$U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$$ conceptually or algebraically.

# Unit 6: Geometric and Physical Optics

## Overview
This unit covers how light behaves as both a **ray** and a **wave**, including **reflection**, **refraction**, image formation by **mirrors** and **lenses**, and wave effects such as **interference** and **diffraction**. On the AP exam, students must connect diagrams, qualitative reasoning, and equations to explain how light travels, bends, forms images, and produces bright and dark patterns.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Reflection** | Light bouncing off a surface so that the **angle of incidence** equals the **angle of reflection** | Frequently tested with ray diagrams and surface geometry |
| **Refraction** | Light changing direction when it moves between media with different optical properties | Central to predicting bending of light and image formation |
| **Snell’s Law** | Quantitative rule relating incident and refracted angles in two media | Essential for solving boundary-crossing problems |
| **Index of Refraction** | A measure of how much light slows in a medium, defined by $$n = \frac{c}{v}$$ | Connects wave speed, bending, and optical density |
| **Thin Lenses** | Curved transparent objects that converge or diverge light rays | Used to find image location, type, orientation, and magnification |
| **Spherical Mirrors** | Concave and convex mirrors that form images by reflection | Common AP problems involve sign conventions and ray tracing |
| **Interference** | Superposition of light waves producing constructive and destructive patterns | Key to understanding bright and dark fringes |
| **Diffraction / Double-Slit** | Spreading and overlapping of waves after passing through openings | Important physical optics topic showing light’s wave nature |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Light encounters boundary or obstacle] --> B{What happens?}
    B --> C[Reflection at surface]
    B --> D[Refraction into new medium]
    B --> E[Passes through lens or reflects from mirror]
    B --> F[Diffraction through slit or around edge]

    C --> G[Use law of reflection]
    D --> H[Use Snell's law and index of refraction]
    E --> I[Trace principal rays]
    I --> J[Locate image]
    J --> K[Determine real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or reduced]
    F --> L[Waves overlap]
    L --> M[Interference pattern forms]
    M --> N[Use path difference or fringe equations]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Rule** | **Expression or Statement** | **Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Law of Reflection** | $$\theta_i = \theta_r$$ | Predicts the reflected ray direction |
| **Index of Refraction** | $$n = \frac{c}{v}$$ | Relates light speed in a medium to vacuum speed |
| **Snell’s Law** | $$n_1 \sin \theta_1 = n_2 \sin \theta_2$$ | Determines refraction angle |
| **Critical Angle** | $$\sin \theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \quad \text{for} \quad n_1 > n_2$$ | Used for **total internal reflection** |
| **Mirror / Lens Equation** | $$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$$ | Finds image distance |
| **Magnification** | $$m = \frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}$$ | Gives image size and orientation |
| **Wave Speed Relationship** | $$v = f\lambda$$ | Helps connect frequency, wavelength, and medium changes |
| **Young’s Double-Slit Bright Fringe** | $$d \sin \theta = m\lambda$$ | Gives angles for constructive interference |
| **Double-Slit Dark Fringe** | $$d \sin \theta = \left(m+\frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$$ | Gives angles for destructive interference |
| **Small-Angle Fringe Position** | $$y_m \approx \frac{m\lambda L}{d}$$ | Finds fringe spacing on a distant screen |
| **Diffraction Grating / Single-Slit Minimum Idea** | For minima in single-slit diffraction: $$a \sin \theta = m\lambda, \quad m=1,2,3,\dots$$ | Predicts dark regions from diffraction |

### Sign conventions to know
- For **converging lenses** and **concave mirrors**, $$f > 0$$.
- For **diverging lenses** and **convex mirrors**, $$f < 0$$.
- A **real image** has $$d_i > 0$$; a **virtual image** has $$d_i < 0$$.
- If $$m > 0$$, the image is **upright**; if $$m < 0$$, the image is **inverted**.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Topic** | **Geometric Optics** | **Physical Optics** | **Key Connection** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Model of light** | Treats light as rays | Treats light as waves | Same light can require different models depending on the phenomenon |
| **Main phenomena** | Reflection, refraction, image formation | Interference, diffraction | AP questions may ask which model best explains an observation |
| **Typical tools** | Ray diagrams, Snell’s law, lens/mirror equations | Path difference, wavelength, fringe equations | Both often involve angles and geometry |
| **Evidence about light** | Rays explain direction and images | Waves explain bright/dark patterns | Double-slit experiment strongly supports wave behavior |

### Lens vs. Mirror image formation

| **Optical Element** | **Converging Type** | **Diverging Type** | **Typical Image Possibilities** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lens** | Convex lens | Concave lens | Can form real or virtual images depending on object position |
| **Mirror** | Concave mirror | Convex mirror | Concave can form real or virtual; convex forms virtual, reduced images |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing the **angle with the surface** and the **angle with the normal**. In optics equations, angles are measured from the **normal**.
- Forgetting that when light enters a medium with **higher index of refraction**, its **speed decreases** and it bends **toward the normal**.
- Mixing up **real** and **virtual** images: a real image forms where rays actually converge, while a virtual image forms where rays only appear to originate.
- Using lens/mirror equations correctly but ignoring the meaning of the sign of $$d_i$$ or $$m$$.
- Assuming diffraction and interference require separate ideas; on the AP exam, **diffraction spreads waves**, making **interference patterns** possible.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can apply the **law of reflection** and correctly measure angles from the **normal**.
- [ ] I can use $$n = \frac{c}{v}$$ and explain how light speed and wavelength change in a new medium.
- [ ] I can solve refraction problems with $$n_1 \sin \theta_1 = n_2 \sin \theta_2$$.
- [ ] I can explain and calculate **critical angle** and **total internal reflection**.
- [ ] I can draw principal rays for **lenses** and **mirrors** and identify image characteristics.
- [ ] I can use $$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$$ and $$m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}$$ with correct sign conventions.
- [ ] I can distinguish when **geometric optics** or **wave optics** is the better model.
- [ ] I can describe and calculate the bright and dark fringes in the **double-slit experiment** using $$d \sin \theta = m\lambda$$ and related relationships.

# Unit 7: Quantum, Atomic, and Nuclear Physics

## Overview
This unit introduces the **quantum** and **nuclear** ideas that classical physics cannot explain, including the **photoelectric effect**, **matter waves**, **atomic energy levels**, **radioactive decay**, and **nuclear reactions**. On the AP exam, these topics often test your ability to connect **models**, **graphs**, and **equations** to physical meaning rather than just compute answers.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Photoelectric effect** | Emission of electrons from a metal when light of sufficiently high frequency strikes it | Tests the idea that light is quantized into **photons** and that energy depends on **frequency**, not intensity |
| **Photon energy** | Light energy carried in packets with energy $$E = hf$$ | Essential for solving threshold frequency, work function, and emitted electron energy questions |
| **de Broglie wavelength** | Matter has wave properties with wavelength $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$ | Used to compare wave behavior of particles with different momentum |
| **Atomic energy levels** | Electrons in atoms occupy discrete allowed energies | Explains emission and absorption spectra and why atoms produce line spectra instead of continuous spectra |
| **Bohr model** | A simplified atomic model with quantized electron energy levels | Common AP context for transitions, photon emission, and energy differences |
| **Radioactive decay** | Spontaneous transformation of unstable nuclei | Students must identify decay type and conserve **mass number** and **atomic number** in nuclear equations |
| **Half-life** | Time required for half of a radioactive sample to decay | Frequently tested with decay graphs, fractions remaining, and exponential reasoning |
| **Mass-energy equivalence** | Mass can be converted to energy according to $$E = mc^2$$ | Critical for nuclear binding energy, fission, fusion, and reaction energy calculations |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Light incident on metal] --> B{Is photon frequency above threshold?}
    B -->|No| C[No electrons emitted]
    B -->|Yes| D[Electrons emitted]
    D --> E[Photon energy given by $$E = hf$$]
    E --> F[Some energy used to overcome work function]
    F --> G[Remaining energy becomes electron kinetic energy]

    H[Excited atom or nucleus] --> I[Transition to lower energy state]
    I --> J[Energy released as photon or particle]

    K[Unstable nucleus] --> L[Radioactive decay]
    L --> M[Alpha, beta, or gamma emission]
    M --> N[New nucleus formed]
    N --> O[Mass difference may correspond to released energy]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Relationship** | **Expression / Rule** | **What to Know** |
|---|---|---|
| **Photon energy** | $$E = hf$$ | Photon energy increases with **frequency** |
| **Speed of light relation** | $$c = f\lambda$$ | Connects wavelength and frequency for electromagnetic waves |
| **Photoelectric equation** | $$K_{\max} = hf - \phi$$ | Maximum electron kinetic energy equals photon energy minus **work function** |
| **Threshold frequency** | $$f_0 = \frac{\phi}{h}$$ | No photoelectrons are emitted for $$f < f_0$$ |
| **Electron kinetic energy** | $$K_{\max} = eV_s$$ | If stopping potential is given, use it to find maximum kinetic energy |
| **de Broglie wavelength** | $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$$ | Larger momentum means shorter wavelength |
| **Energy of emitted or absorbed photon** | $$\Delta E = hf$$ | Photon energy matches the difference between atomic energy levels |
| **Mass-energy equivalence** | $$E = mc^2$$ | A small mass defect corresponds to large energy |
| **Radioactive decay model** | $$N = N_0\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$$ | Amount remaining after time $$t$$ depends on half-life |
| **Alpha decay rule** | $$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$ | Mass number decreases by $$4$$, atomic number by $$2$$ |
| **Beta minus decay rule** | $$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + ^{0}_{-1}e$$ | Mass number stays the same, atomic number increases by $$1$$ |
| **Gamma decay rule** | $$^{A}_{Z}X^{*} \rightarrow ^{A}_{Z}X + \gamma$$ | No change in mass number or atomic number |

### Must-know qualitative rules
- **Increasing light intensity** increases the **number** of emitted photoelectrons, but not their maximum kinetic energy, if frequency stays fixed above threshold.
- **Increasing light frequency** increases the **energy per photon** and therefore can increase emitted electron kinetic energy.
- **Atomic spectra** are **discrete** because atomic energies are quantized.
- In **nuclear reactions**, conserve both **mass number** and **atomic number**.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Comparison** | **Concept 1** | **Concept 2** | **Key AP Connection** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Intensity vs frequency in photoelectric effect** | **Intensity** changes number of photons arriving each second | **Frequency** changes energy per photon | AP questions often ask which one affects electron emission and kinetic energy |
| **Classical wave model vs quantum model of light** | Predicts energy should depend on intensity | Shows energy is quantized as $$E = hf$$ | The photoelectric effect supports the quantum model |
| **Atomic transitions vs nuclear transitions** | Involve electron energy levels and usually lower energies | Involve changes in the nucleus and much larger energies | Helps distinguish spectra questions from nuclear reaction questions |
| **Fission vs fusion** | Heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei | Light nuclei combine into heavier nucleus | Both can release energy through mass defect and binding energy changes |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **light intensity** with **light frequency** in the **photoelectric effect**. Only frequency determines whether electrons are emitted and their maximum kinetic energy.
- Forgetting that **below threshold frequency**, no electrons are emitted no matter how intense the light is.
- Mixing up **atomic number** and **mass number** when balancing **nuclear equations**.
- Assuming **gamma decay** changes the identity of the nucleus. It does not change either atomic number or mass number.
- Using **continuous-energy** thinking for atoms; on the AP exam, electrons in atoms occupy **discrete** energy levels.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] Explain how the **photoelectric effect** supports the particle model of light.
- [ ] Use $$E = hf$$ and $$c = f\lambda$$ to relate photon energy, frequency, and wavelength.
- [ ] Apply $$K_{\max} = hf - \phi$$ to determine whether photoelectrons are emitted and how energetic they are.
- [ ] Calculate or compare **de Broglie wavelengths** using $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$.
- [ ] Describe how **atomic energy level transitions** produce **emission** or **absorption** spectra.
- [ ] Balance **alpha**, **beta**, and **gamma** decay equations using conservation of mass number and atomic number.
- [ ] Solve half-life problems using fractions remaining or $$N = N_0\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$$.
- [ ] Explain how **mass defect** leads to released energy through $$E = mc^2$$ in **fission** or **fusion**.
